text: Every REST Message you built in Chapter 2 worked, because you tested the happy path — the external system answered with HTTP 200 and clean JSON every time. In production, running unattended for years, that is the least representative thing that happens. The system you depend on will go down, its credentials will expire, its API will change without telling you, and it will get overloaded by traffic that has nothing to do with you. None of that is a bug in your code — it's the normal operating condition of depending on a system you don't control, and happy-path-only code was never asked 'what if this fails.'

Look at this block: it calls the WeatherAPI REST Message, parses the body as JSON, and reads a nested field, with no status-code check anywhere. It assumes the call returned 200, assumes the body is valid JSON, and assumes that field still exists in the exact shape it did when the script was written. That is three silent assumptions stacked on top of each other, and any one of them failing takes down the whole block with an unhandled exception instead of a controlled response.

Real integrations fail in four recurring ways, and naming them is most of the design work. The external system can be unreachable — a network or DNS failure, or the service itself down, so the call simply times out. Authentication can expire mid-session, since an OAuth token that was valid an hour ago silently isn't anymore. The response shape can change, when the external team renames or moves a field with no warning. And the system can rate-limit you with an HTTP 429, which isn't an outage — it's the system protecting itself and expecting you to slow down, not retry harder.

If none of that is handled, ServiceNow doesn't quietly absorb the problem. An uncaught exception in a business rule can abort the transaction it ran inside. A flow action with no defined error path stops the entire run, visible only in that flow's execution log to someone who goes looking. A scheduled job can stop partway through with nothing recorded and no one notified. 'It failed' is true, but why gets left for whoever discovers the outage later — usually a user reporting that something just doesn't work.

The design habit that fixes this is simple to state: treat failure as the default expectation, not the exception, and decide the right response for each category before writing any error-handling code. A timeout or server error is often worth retrying. A 429 means back off and retry slower. A client error means the request itself is wrong, and retrying it just repeats the same failure. Next lesson turns that distinction into a real retry strategy, built around exponential backoff and idempotency.
